stories.title: Madewell To Open New Store at Tishman Speyer’s 1 Rockefeller Plaza
stories.excerpt: Famed denim and clothing brand Madewell is opening a new store at Tishman Speyer’s 1 Rockefeller Plaza, the landlord announced Thursday. The retailer signed a 7,340-square-foot lease at the Midtown landmark, where its new space will open in 2027. The asking rent and the length of the lease were not disclosed, but the average asking rent for retail space in Midtown Plaza District was $2,540 per square foot during the second quarter of 2026, according to CBRE data. “Rockefeller Center continues to attract brands that shape culture and consumer behavior globally,” EB Kelly, senior managing director at Tishman Speyer and head of Rockefeller Center, said in a statement. “Madewell’s decision to establish a presence here reinforces the center’s unique ability to combine iconic New York identity with modern cultural relevance.” Newmark brokered the deal for Madewell, while Tishman Speyer was repped in-house by Lucy Phillips. Newmark did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Madewell’s new store at Rockefeller Center will be its eighth location in New York City. “We’re excited to be part of Rockefeller Center, one of New York’s most iconic retail destinations,” Garrett Putney, senior vice president of retail at Madewell, said in a statement. “This store represents an important milestone for Madewell, giving us the opportunity to bring our full brand experience to life in a space that reflects our commitment to quality, style and community.” Built in 1937, 1 Rockefeller Plaza is a 34-story office, dining and shopping center located between West 48th and West 49th streets in Midtown. Office tenants in the building include real estate investment trust Chimera Investment Corporation and investment firm Ulysses Management, while clothing shop Alex Mill has a ground-floor location there. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Madewell signs 7,340-sf lease at Tishman Speyer's 1 Rockefeller Plaza, opening 2027.
Midtown retail asking rent $2,540/sf (Q2 2026); flagship location signals tenant confidence.
Cultural retail anchor reinforces trophy office/mixed-use asset value and foot traffic.
stories.summary: Madewell leased 7,340 square feet at 1 Rockefeller Plaza in Midtown Manhattan, with the store opening in 2027. Average asking rent in the Midtown Plaza District is $2,540 per square foot. The deal reflects continued anchor-tenant interest in flagship Rockefeller Center locations despite broader office headwinds.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance. However, strong retail leasing in trophy Manhattan addresses signals stable foot traffic and mixed-use viability in Midtown, supporting residual demand for nearby apartment conversions or premium rental units targeting retail/office workers. Indirect positive signal for residential density near retail nodes.

stories.title: KKR Names Sam Caven, Marshall Nevins New Co-Heads of Acquisitions
stories.excerpt: KKR has appointed Sam Caven and Marshall Nevins co-heads of acquisitions for the Americas, Commercial Observer can first report. Nevins joins KKR from Blackstone, where he was a managing director, leading investments across multiple real estate strategies. Caven has led investment activity across KKR’s U.S. real estate funds since 2024 and previously spent 13 years at Starwood Capital. The new co-heads now join Brett Kelly and Michael Osborne, co-heads of KKR’s real estate equity asset management business, with all four reporting up to Justin Pattner, head of equity for the Americas. “We pride ourselves on continuing to evolve, and sometimes the more profound changes around businesses present themselves as people-related changes,” Pattner said. “We’ve been investing, harvesting, and trying to figure out what our organizational structure should look like on a go-forward basis so that we can maintain performance and grow well into the future, and this was a great time to make those changes.” Nevins’ first day was August 12, and so those changes are now up and running. “As a firm, we’re big believers in if you can find the right co-head model — because people have different perspectives and different strengths — and as long as you have the right organizational structure and the right incentive model, you can be in a situation where one-plus-one is greater than two,” Pattner said. “So, it’s a case of the right time, right people, and we’re pretty excited.” San Francisco-based Caven brings 19 years of experience to his new role. At Starwood, he led acquisitions and dispositions of office, industrial and residential assets and also worked on the formation of Starwood Waypoint Homes and Starwood Real Estate Income Trust. bullets: KKR appoints Sam Caven and Marshall Nevins co-heads of acquisitions for Americas.
Nevins hired from Blackstone (managing director); Caven previously at Starwood Capital (13 years).
Organizational restructure signals KKR scaling acquisition engine post-harvest cycle.
stories.summary: KKR named Sam Caven and Marshall Nevins as co-heads of acquisitions for the Americas, effective August 12. Nevins joins from Blackstone and Caven comes from 13 years at Starwood Capital. The move is part of KKR's broader effort to evolve its organizational structure and maintain performance in equity investing.
stories.impact: Signals KKR is aggressive in acquisition sourcing across real estate, including multifamily. Starwood Capital and Blackstone veterans bring deep multifamily expertise; expect KKR to accelerate deal flow, potentially competing harder for trophy and value-add apartment portfolios. Institutional capital deployment momentum favors well-positioned assets and sponsors in core markets.

stories.title: Motek Founders Sign NoMad Lease For New Offshoot Restaurant
stories.excerpt: Happy Corner Hospitality has signed a lease in Manhattan’s NoMad neighborhood for an offshoot of their Motek concept. Known as Yalla Motek, the restaurant group took 2,500 square feet at David and Jack Israel’s 1147 Broadway, which will be the new Mediterranean chain’s first location in New York City and second in the U.S. after opening in Aventura, Fla., in 2022, according to Happy Corner. Happy Corner did not immediately disclose the asking rent, length of the lease or any brokers involved in the deal, but the average retail asking rent along the nearby retail corridor of Broadway from 14th to 23rd Streets was $371 per square foot in the second quarter of 2026, according to a report from CBRE. “We always knew New York was the right city to truly introduce the brand,” Charlie Levy, founder of Happy Corner, said in a statement. “Its energy, diversity and fast pace make it the perfect fit. … This is just the beginning — we’re planning five locations in New York with a vision of growing to 20 locations over the next three years and sharing our passion for Mediterranean street food with even more communities.” Motek itself has four locations in New York City, with the most recent lease being for 184 Bleecker Street in Greenwich Village in November 2025. Carolina Aziz of KSR has represented both the Israels and Motek in previous deals, including negotiating on behalf of Motek at 184 Bleecker, but did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Motek has made a name for itself whipping up Mediterranean street food dishes with whole ingredients and free of seed oils. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Happy Corner Hospitality leases 2,500 sf in NoMad (1147 Broadway) for Yalla Motek.
Plans five NYC locations in near term, 20 total within three years.
Broadway 14th–23rd retail corridor asking rent $371/sf (Q2 2026).
stories.summary: Happy Corner Hospitality signed a lease for 2,500 square feet at 1147 Broadway in Manhattan's NoMad for Yalla Motek, a Mediterranean restaurant concept. The company plans to open five locations in New York and 20 nationwide within three years. Average retail asking rent along Broadway (14th–23rd Streets) is $371 per square foot.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact. However, aggressive restaurant expansion in NoMad/Flatiron corridor signals strong foot-traffic recovery and restaurant-as-amenity viability in that submarket, supporting rental demand among young professionals. Retail activation supports residential leasing momentum in NoMad and adjacent neighborhoods; validates mixed-use density play.

stories.title: ParkProperty Acquires 280-Unit Buckhead Apartment Community
stories.excerpt: ParkProperty Capital acquired The Jane, a 280-unit multifamily in the Brookwood district of Atlanta, adjacent to Buckhead. The property was traded for $75 million. CWS Capital Partners was the seller. The property was named after the local golf legend Bobby Jones’ putter, Calamity Jane. Brookwood sits adjacent to the Bobby Jones Golf Course. Once called Marquis at Buckhead, The Jane is located steps away from the Beltline Northside Trail along Colonial Homes Drive Northwest. The community features one- and two-bedroom floor plans. Amenities include a saltwater pool, two sundecks, outdoor sporting and recreation area, and a regulation-size Bocce Ball court . ParkProperty Capital plans to renovate the community’s interiors to better align with the property’s branding and pay tribute to its contemporary Southern exterior architecture. ParkProperty Capital purchased an adjacent multifamily property, The Monroe, in 2022. The company owns additional multifamily assets in U.S. metros such as Houston, Charlotte, Austin, Seattle and Phoenix. The post ParkProperty Acquires 280-Unit Buckhead Apartment Community appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: ParkProperty Capital acquired The Jane, 280-unit Brookwood district (Buckhead-adjacent) Atlanta for $75M.
Property features 1-2 BR plans; ParkProperty owns adjacent Monroe property and holds Atlanta portfolio.
Interior renovation planned; Brookwood location near Bobby Jones Golf Course and Beltline Northside Trail.
stories.summary: ParkProperty Capital acquired The Jane, a 280-unit multifamily community in Atlanta's Brookwood district (adjacent to Buckhead), for $75 million from CWS Capital Partners. The property will undergo interior renovations. ParkProperty also owns The Monroe nearby and operates multifamily assets in Houston, Charlotte, Austin, Seattle, and Phoenix.
stories.impact: Signals continued institutional appetite for Buckhead-adjacent Atlanta submarket. At $268K/unit, pricing reflects stabilized fundamentals and walkable urban positioning near Beltline. ParkProperty's value-add playbook (renovation + adjacent ownership) demonstrates confidence in Brookwood's rental demand and lifestyle amenity value. Suggests healthy rent-growth outlook for quality product in Atlanta's urban core submarkets.

stories.title: Sixth Street Pays $190M for Key West Resort
stories.excerpt: Sixth Street acquired the Pier House Resort & Spa, a 142-room, luxury oceanfront resort in Key West, Florida, for $190 million from Braemar Hotels & Resorts. Sixth Street completed the transaction in partnership with Riller Capital. Financing for the transaction was provided by Starwood Property Trust. Situated on five acres at 1 Duval Street, Pier House is located on the waterfront at the gateway to Key West’s Duval Street. Amenities include two oceanfront dining venues, a full-service spa, fitness center, oceanfront pool, 75 linear feet of private beach frontage, and approximately 3,000 square feet of meeting and event space. Sixth Street Real Estate invests directly in properties, provides solutions across the capital structure—including equity, preferred equity, and debt—and partners with sector-related operating businesses. The firm’s real estate investments span a wide range of asset classes, including residential, office, hospitality, industrial, data centers, retail, and other specialized sectors. The post Sixth Street Pays $190M for Key West Resort appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Sixth Street acquired Pier House Resort & Spa, 142-room Key West oceanfront, for $190M.
Financed by Starwood Property Trust; partnered with Riller Capital.
Luxury hospitality asset on 5 acres, 75 linear feet private beach; gateway to Duval Street.
stories.summary: Sixth Street Partners acquired the Pier House Resort & Spa, a 142-room luxury oceanfront resort in Key West, for $190 million from Braemar Hotels & Resorts. Starwood Property Trust provided financing, and Riller Capital partnered on the deal. The property sits on five acres at the gateway to Duval Street.
stories.impact: Not relevant to multifamily development. Hospitality-focused transaction with no bearing on apartment supply, demand, or capital flows. Demonstrates continued institutional capital into premium resort/lodging, but distinct from rental housing underwriting, financing, and market cycles.

stories.title: Xebec Snags Financing for 687K-SF Savannah-Area Industrial Development
stories.excerpt: Xebec closed on $30.49 million in joint-venture equity alongside $39.95 million in construction financing for Black Creek Commerce Center, a three-building Class A industrial development in Black Creek, Georgia. not far from Savannah. JLL secured the construction loan from Seacoast Bank and placed the joint-venture equity with a private investment group. Scheduled to deliver in the third quarter of 2027, the 687,890-square-foot development will feature three buildings spanning 219,170, 284,580 and 184,140 square feet. The development has direct access to U.S. Highway 80, providing immediate connectivity to Interstate 16 and the broader Atlanta market. The Xebec holds a right of first refusal on Phase II, an adjacent 77-acre parcel, through April 2027. The JLL Capital Markets team representing the developer was led by Bobby Norwood and Mark Sixour, along with Britton Burdette, Jim Freeman, Kelsey Bawcombe and Austin Smith. The post Xebec Snags Financing for 687K-SF Savannah-Area Industrial Development appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Xebec closed $30.49M equity + $39.95M construction financing for Black Creek Commerce Center near Savannah.
687,890-sf Class A industrial (3 buildings), delivery Q3 2027; direct I-16/Atlanta access.
Seacoast Bank provided construction loan; Xebec holds ROFR on adjacent 77-acre Phase II through Apr 2027.
stories.summary: Xebec secured $30.49 million in joint-venture equity and $39.95 million in construction financing for Black Creek Commerce Center, a three-building Class A industrial development near Savannah delivering Q3 2027. The 687,890-square-foot project features buildings ranging 184K–285K sf and direct I-16 connectivity to Atlanta. Xebec holds a right of first refusal on a 77-acre Phase II parcel.
stories.impact: Signals industrial capital and construction financing availability in Southeast logistics corridors. While not multifamily, Savannah area's industrial acceleration (port growth, distribution hub status) drives in-migration and job growth, strengthening residential demand. Xebec's multi-phase strategy and Phase II optionality suggest long-term developer confidence in Savannah submarket, likely supporting future multifamily anchor projects nearby.

stories.title: Producer Prices Flat in July as Goods Costs Fall
stories.excerpt: U.S. producer prices were unchanged in July as declining goods costs balanced out increases across services and construction, according to data released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.  The Producer Price Index for final demand remained flat on a seasonally adjusted basis after edging down 0.1% in June and advancing 0.5% in May. Over the 12 months ending in July, unadjusted final demand prices increased 4.7%.  Excluding volatile food, energy, and trade services components, the core final demand index rose 0.4% in July following a modest 0.1% tick higher in June. On an annual basis, the index for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services gained 4.7%.  Final-demand goods prices declined 0.7% in July after falling 1.4% in June. Energy prices dropped 3.1%, led by a 5.7% decrease in gasoline. Food prices declined 0.9%, while prices for goods excluding food and energy edged up 0.1%. Those declines were offset by a 0.2% increase in final-demand services and a 2.2% advance in construction prices.  Services excluding trade, transportation and warehousing  increased 0.6%. Portfolio-management prices surged 6.5%, while margins rose for several retail categories. Freight-trucking prices declined 1.8%, and trade-service margins slipped 0.1%.  The report may reduce the urgency for a September rate increase, but the strength in services and construction gives policymakers reason to remain cautious about declaring inflation contained.  The post Producer Prices Flat in July as Goods Costs Fall appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: July PPI flat seasonally adjusted; goods prices -0.7%, services +0.2%, construction +2.2%.
12-month PPI +4.7%; core final demand (ex food, energy) +4.7% annually.
Energy down 3.1%, gasoline -5.7%; construction costs accelerating despite goods deflation.
stories.summary: U.S. producer prices were flat on a seasonally adjusted basis in July after declining 0.1% in June. Over 12 months, final demand prices rose 4.7%. Goods prices fell 0.7% in July (driven by energy and food), but construction prices advanced 2.2% and services rose 0.2%. Core inflation (ex food, energy, trade services) increased 4.7% year-over-year.
stories.impact: Construction cost inflation remains sticky at +2.2% despite goods deflation, pressuring multifamily development budgeting and feasibility. Core services inflation at 4.7% annually suggests labor costs remain elevated. While energy/commodity declines offer modest relief, developers should expect continued labor and trade cost resistance through 2027 delivery windows, compressing margins or requiring rent-growth assumptions to support underwriting on new starts.

stories.title: Walker Webcast: McKinsey’s Aditya Sanghvi Discusses Why and How Agentic AI Can Be Tailor-Made for Rental Housing
stories.excerpt: Artificial intelligence, particularly the agentic kind, could help rental housing owners and operators automate tasks, coordinate maintenance and improve resident retention. But getting there involves more than installing a new technology. “I would put out there that rental housing is perfect for AI,” said McKinsey & Co. senior partner Aditya Sanghvi, a leader of the firm’s global real estate practice. Sanghvi spoke at Walker & Dunlop’s recent annual convention in Sun Valley, Idaho, in a session broadcast Aug. 12 as a Walker Webcast. During the session, Sanghvi discussed why rental housing is well-suited to agentic AI, why adoption remains slow and what CEOs can do to get more value from the technology. Rental Housing Is Built for Agentic AI Unlike generative AI, which responds to human prompts, agentic AI is given a goal. The agent then plans and executes the tasks needed to achieve it. Multiple agents can also coordinate specialized processes. Sanghvi said that the technology perfectly matches property management, as the industry relies on numerous relatively simple tasks that become complicated when residents, property managers and vendors intersect. The result can be “dead zones,” the unfulfilled maintenance tickets, unanswered calls and missed follow-ups that can erode the resident experience. Agentic AI can help fill those gaps. In a maintenance situation, for example, one agent could triage requests, another could coordinate vendors, and another could handle scheduling. A separate agent could identify recurring problems and improve future decisions. Agentic AI could also improve lease conversions, renewals, collections and other repetitive processes. Over time, agents can learn from repeated decisions and become more effective. This doesn’t mean that humans are eliminated. “Humans are essential for the loop of every agent AI process,” Sanghvi said. Humans still outperform agents on many tasks. Also, agents can’t be held accountable.” Adoption Remains
bullets: McKinsey senior partner Aditya Sanghvi: agentic AI ideal for rental housing automation.
AI can coordinate maintenance, automate tasks, improve resident retention and resolve 'dead zones.'
Adoption remains slow despite operational fit; CEO involvement critical to value capture.
stories.summary: McKinsey's Aditya Sanghvi discussed agentic AI applications in rental housing at Walker & Dunlop's convention. Unlike generative AI, agentic AI takes a goal and plans/executes tasks autonomously. The technology suits property management because it handles routine tasks complicated by resident-manager-vendor intersections and can resolve operational 'dead zones' (missed maintenance, unanswered calls).
stories.impact: Highlights emerging operational efficiency opportunity for multifamily operators but signals adoption lag remains a barrier. Early movers (large platforms with capital for tech integration) will gain cost and retention advantages; this widens the performance gap between sophisticated operators and smaller/independent players. Relevant for value-add and stabilized-asset underwriting: tech-enabled ops can justify higher prices and support rent-growth leverage.

stories.title: The Schedule C Trap: Why Your Biggest Deal This Year Might Be With the IRS
stories.excerpt: In real estate, we’re obsessed with the big numbers, what we “gross.” We talk about ‘GCI’ like it’s the only number that matters. We celebrate the $50 million year, the record-breaking penthouse sale, and the expansion into new markets (hello, California for SERHANT.!). But, after the 1099s are issued and the dust settles, a lot of agents realize that while they were busy selling the dream, they were living a tax reality that is — to put it bluntly — inefficient. The problem with ‘playing small’ Most agents start as “solopreneurs.” It’s you, your phone and a dream. You file as a sole proprietor because it’s easy. You run everything through a Schedule C because that’s what your first mentor told you to do. But here’s the truth: What worked for you when you were doing three deals a year is a financial impediment once you hit the big leagues. I call it the “Schedule C Trap.” When you’re a high-earner filing as a sole proprietor, you aren’t just paying income tax — you’re getting hammered by self-employment taxes on every single dollar you earn. We’re talking about a potential $10,000 to $30,000 “convenience fee” that you’re effectively handing to the government every year simply because you haven’t structured your business like a business. In 2026, the complexity has only ramped up. Between the shifting SALT cap limits and the new surcharges on high-income filers in hubs like New York, the “wait and see” approach to accounting is no longer a viable strategy — it’s a massive liability. You’re digging through glove boxes for gas receipts, charity donation receipts, scrolling through Venmo history to remember if that “lunch meeting” was for a client or a cousin, and praying your accountant doesn’t fire you. bullets: Tax advisory piece on Schedule C sole-proprietor trap for high-earning real estate agents.
Self-employment tax burden ($10K–$30K+) erodes income for agents exceeding $1M-2M GCI.
Entity structure optimization (S-corp, LLC) can recover 15–20% net income.
stories.summary: An opinion piece discusses tax inefficiency in real estate sales for solopreneurs filing Schedule C. High-earning agents face self-employment tax penalties on every dollar earned, potentially costing $10,000–$30,000+. The author advocates for LLC or S-corp structures to recapture 15–20% of net income once GCI exceeds certain thresholds.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily development underwriting or capital markets. Tangentially signals agent profitability compression, which could marginally reduce discretionary investment capital for real estate investors who are also sales professionals. No material impact on apartment supply, demand, or financing fundamentals.

stories.title: Luxury Condo Sales in Manhattan Rise Post-Pied-à-Terre Rollout
stories.excerpt: The luxury pied-à-terre is alive and well, despite any efforts to stifle — or excessively tax — it. While the second week of August saw a Staten Island Supreme Court judge block the rollout of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax — a controversial surcharge on second homes worth more than $5 million — the first week of the month saw a year-over-year rise in such sales. From Aug. 1 to Aug. 7, there were 16 contracts signed above $5 million, a 7 percent year-over-year increase when compared to the same week in 2025, according to data from Corcoran Sunshine shared exclusively with Commercial Observer. In addition, since the passage of the tax some 16 weeks ago, sales of condos, co-ops and townhomes worth more than $5 million are up 1 percent from those 16 weeks last year, and up 3 percent versus the five-year average, the data shows. Overall, Manhattan saw 302 sales over $5 million from April 18 to Aug. 7, versus 268 sales tracked from Jan. 31 to April 17. For that same time period of April to August, sales of homes worth between $5 million and $15 million are up 2 percent year-over-year, while sales of homes worth between $15 million and $25 million are up 8 percent. Commercial Observer However, homes valued at higher prices, like $25 million and more, are down 20 percent year-over-year — but that doesn’t mean they aren’t selling. The largest contract signed during the week of Aug. 1 to Aug. 7 was a full-floor residence at 1122 Madison Avenue worth $40.5 million. Sentiment around Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax has certainly been mixed since the legislature was passed at the end of May, especially after the mayor posted a controversial video that called out Citadel CEO Ken Griffin by name over his $238 million Manhattan penthouse and caused some to speculate that Griffin might abandon the planned tower Citadel was building in Midtown and focus instead on Florida. But sales haven’t halted yet, despite owners becoming increasingly frustrated with the system.
bullets: Manhattan luxury condo sales ($5M+) up 7% YoY week of Aug 1–7; 16 contracts signed.
Since pied-à-terre tax passage (16 weeks), sales $5M+ up 1% YoY, +3% vs 5-yr avg.
Aug 1–Aug 7: 302 sales $5M+ vs 268 Jan 31–Apr 17; pied-à-terre tax blocked Aug 2025.
stories.summary: Manhattan luxury condo sales above $5 million rose 7 percent year-over-year for the week of August 1–7, with 16 contracts signed. Since the pied-à-terre tax passage 16 weeks ago, sales above $5 million are up 1 percent YoY and 3 percent versus the five-year average. A judge blocked the tax rollout in mid-August; $5M–$15M sales are up 2 percent YoY.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily impact, but signals strong high-end condo demand in Manhattan despite tax headwinds. Tax uncertainty removal and legal block may accelerate ultra-luxury and pied-à-terre closings, reinforcing Manhattan's wealth magnet position and the resilience of premium residential. For multifamily, this underscores persistent capital flow to NYC and validates premium/luxury apartment positioning in Manhattan. Indirectly supports rental demand from wealth migrants and lifestyle-focused high-income renters.
